messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Jasper is a 56-year-old married musician who, eighteen months ago, was sexually assaulted by a colleague after a performance. He had stayed behind to pack his equipment when the other man cornered him in the green room. The man, who had been drinking, was someone Jasper had considered a friend. What Jasper remembers most clearly is the cologne his attacker wore—a sharp, woody scent that he had complimented earlier that evening. Other moments of the assault are fragmented: the pressure of a hand over his mouth, the sound of a chair scraping against the floor. But the sequence is lost to him. He cannot tell himself a coherent story of what happened; when he tries, the memory breaks apart before it reaches its end, and he pushes it away, deliberately shutting it down before he can fully recall it.

In the months that followed, Jasper began to notice changes in how he moved through the world. Sudden movements by others put him immediately on guard. A hand reaching for a wallet on the subway, a child darting across his path in the park—his body would lock, his heart hammering. He became irritable, snapping at his wife for small things like leaving a cabinet door open, and once shouting at a sound technician who tapped him on the shoulder without warning. What frightened him most was his own anger. He had never allowed himself to feel or express anger before, and now it seemed to live just beneath his skin. He began suppressing it deliberately, clenching his jaw and walking away whenever he felt the heat rise, because he was certain that if he let it out, he would lose control completely and hurt someone.

The memory itself fed his vigilance. Each time he tried to recall the assault, the blank spaces in his memory felt threatening—he was sure those missing moments held something terrible that he could not face, and this certainty kept his body in a state of low-grade alarm. He found himself only feeling safe in a very limited number of places: his home studio, his car, the corner booth at a coffee shop he had been going to for years. Everywhere else felt like potential danger. The smell of cologne in a department store would hit him without warning, and suddenly he would be scanning the room for exits, his pulse roaring in his ears. The threat he felt in those moments would then sharpen his memory of the assault, bringing back the pressure of that hand, the scrape of the chair, even as the full narrative remained out of reach.

Jasper began avoiding people he had socialised with before the event, because being around them meant fielding questions about why he had stopped performing, and the questions themselves felt like a kind of pressure he could not tolerate. He also avoided being around people in authority or uniform. A police officer walking a beat, a security guard at a venue—these figures now made him feel watched and judged, as if they might see something shameful in him. His suppression of anger, in turn, fed his avoidance: after snapping at a former bandmate who had greeted him too enthusiastically at a grocery store, Jasper felt such shame that he stopped answering that friend's calls entirely. The more he avoided, the more his memory of the assault felt both unreal and inescapable—a story he could not tell but could not stop living inside.

The cycle tightened. His vigilance kept his memory fragmented and raw; his fragmented memory kept his vigilance high. He stopped going to rehearsals. He stopped answering messages from the venue bookers who had once kept him employed. His wife found him pacing the living room late at night, unable to explain what he was so afraid of. What finally brought Jasper to seek help was a moment at a wedding reception, when a guest wearing a familiar cologne walked past him and Jasper found himself on the floor, his chair tipped over, his fist pressed against his own chest as if to hold his heart in place. He is terrified that he will never feel safe again, and he is equally terrified of what he might do if he stops holding his anger at bay. He wants to be able to walk into a room without scanning it for exits. He wants to be able to remember his own life.
